rows.intervention: short contact cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen spray gun for 3-5 seconds on 5 macules per patient, once a month until repigmentation, maximum 3 applications
rows.comparator: 88% phenol on 5 other macules in the same patients (row 1); no untreated control
rows.endpoint_definition: grade of improvement in pigmentation per macule 'At the end of the treatment period': excellent >75%, good 51-75%, minimal 26-50%, no response <25%; excellent is partial repigmentation, not complete coverage
rows.arm_result: excellent (>75%) 75/125 (60%); good (51-75%) 20/125 (16%); minimal (26-50%) 15/125 (12%); no response (<25%) 15/125 (12%); signs of repigmentation 110/125 (88%); difference from phenol p<0.05 (test not named)
rows.complete_match: not reported (top grade is '>75%'; no count of macules fully matching surrounding skin)
rows.texture_or_scar: persistent scabbing (scab persisting more than 15 days) 3/125 (2.4%) macules; scarring 0; ulceration 0 (Table 2)
rows.uncertainty: Original publication; a near-identical Clin Dermatol Rev 2021 article (study_id rajegowda2021, already in the ledger) was retracted as a duplicate of it, so the two must not be counted as separate cohorts. Same department and authors as deepadarshan2023, whose ref 15 is a 2022 CO2 laser vs 88% phenol IGH paper by the group; possible shared phenol-arm patients (this study ran June 2017 to May 2018). Follow-up is 3 months with no statement of the interval after the final application; the authors write 'Further studies with longer duration of follow up required to confirm our results'. Nothing on six-month durability. Grading scale has gaps (<25%, 26-50%, 51-75%, >75%: exactly 25%, 50% and 75% fall in no grade); 'no response' is <25% improvement, not zero. Applications were 'once in a month till the repigmentation for maximum 3', but the Abstract calls cryotherapy 'single cryotherapy'; Results say '5 patients in phenol group and 8 patients in cryotherapy group required 2nd application' (counted in patients, although every patient had both arms); no third application is mentioned. Macules within one patient treated as independent; the p<0.05 comparison names no test and does not say whether pairing was accounted for. Abstract says ulceration was 'more common with 88% phenol', but Table 2 shows 0 ulceration in both groups. Table 2 cells were assigned to rows and columns from the PDF text layout [cryotherapy column 3, 5, 0, 0; phenol column 41, 18, 16, 0]; each percentage fits n=125. Mean age 56.5 years, range 30-70 in Results, while inclusion was 18-70. Site percentages 46.6% and 26.6% [fit 14/30 and 8/30 truncated]. Topical 2% mupirocin was advised to 'All the patients'; whether cryotherapy macules received it is not stated. Cryotherapy and phenol may both act partly through post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (Discussion), so early pigment may not be a lasting colour match. How IGH was diagnosed (clinical, dermoscopy or biopsy) not reported. Internal contradiction: Results say 'Signs of repigmentation noted in each macule at the end of 4 weeks in phenol group and 6-8weeks in cryotherapy group', yet Table 1 and the Results report 15/125 cryotherapy macules with 'no repigmentation' and 29/125 phenol macules with 'no response'.
